name: Self-titration (reduced inhalation at higher active-puff conditions)
description: Participants inhaled less smoke from active cigarettes than from position-matched inactive cigarettes, and expired CO fell at higher active-puff conditions — both indicate participants reduced how much they actually inhaled as nominal active dose rose, partially decoupling nominal dose from realized exposure.

name: Expectancy effects on subjective ratings
description: Authors hypothesize that because active puffs were always smoked before inactive puffs, the direct effects of the first two active puffs raised participants' expectation that subsequent puffs were also active — leading them to rate 2, 4, and 6 puffs similarly despite differing cardiovascular responses. Cites prior literature (Camí et al. 1991; Metrik et al. 2009) that subjective responses are more expectancy-sensitive than physiological ones.

name: Tolerance in heavy/daily users may mask subtle dose differences
description: Study limitation raised by authors: because the sample was daily marijuana smokers, tolerance to subjective/performance-impairing effects may make it harder for this population to distinguish subtle differences within a narrow active-dose range. Authors note results might differ in a less-exposed population.

name: Self-titration to similar THC exposure within product form
description: Because 16% vs 24% flower (and 70% vs 90% concentrate) did not produce significantly different blood THC levels, authors suggest users may be self-titrating -- adjusting how much they consume -- to reach a similar target level of exposure as labeled potency rises within a form. This is an inference from an absence of a potency effect, not a directly observed titration behavior (contrast with ramesh-2013-self-titration, where reduced inhalation was directly measured via CO and cigarette weight).

name: Greater tolerance in concentrate users
description: Proposed explanation for why concentrate users, despite ~2.3x higher plasma THC, did not show correspondingly higher subjective intoxication: concentrate users may have greater tolerance to THC's psychoactive effects from more frequent/higher exposure. Explicitly framed by the authors as one of three competing possibilities requiring future research, not a demonstrated mechanism in this study.

name: CB1 receptor saturation / diminishing returns at high THC
description: Second proposed (unproven) explanation: cannabinoid CB1 receptors, as a partial-agonist target of THC, may become saturated at higher THC levels, beyond which additional THC produces diminishing subjective effect. Explicitly speculative in the source.

name: Individual differences in metabolism/sensitivity
description: Third proposed (unproven) explanation: genetic or other pre-existing biological differences in cannabinoid metabolism or sensitivity among users could account for the dissociation between blood THC and subjective intoxication. Explicitly speculative; authors state future research is needed to test all three candidate mechanisms.
